pageInfo.subtitle: Master dynamics, accents, and ghost notes to bring expressiveness and musicality to your playing.
pageInfo.heroDescription: Musical dynamics are what separate mechanical playing from truly expressive guitar work. These exercises develop your ability to control volume, articulate accents, and incorporate ghost notes - essential skills for all genres from funk to fingerstyle to rock.

items.text: Control comes from pick attack angle and force
Use fretting hand pressure to shape sustain
Dynamics should serve the music, not show off technique
Accents come from a slightly wider pick stroke
Ghost notes use minimal fretting pressure and light picking
Practice exaggerating dynamics before making them subtle
Listen critically to how dynamics change the musical feel

exercises.title: Crescendo & Decrescendo
exercises.description: Play a single open string repeatedly with eighth notes for 4 bars. Gradually increase volume (crescendo) over bars 1-2, then gradually decrease (decrescendo) over bars 3-4. Focus on smooth, even volume changes.

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Start at the softest volume you can produce (pianissimo) and grow to the loudest (fortissimo) by the middle, then return. Each note should be slightly different in volume from the last.

exercises.title: Three-Level Dynamics
exercises.description: Play an E minor chord pattern at three distinct volume levels: soft (piano), medium (mezzo-forte), and loud (forte). One bar of each, then switch. Your goal is clear, consistent separation between levels.

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: The hard part is maintaining consistent volume within each level. Record yourself and listen back to check for unwanted volume fluctuations.

exercises.title: Downbeat Accents
exercises.description: Play eighth notes on the A string, accenting every downbeat (beats 1, 2, 3, 4). The accented notes should be distinctly louder than the unaccented notes between them. This creates a strong rhythmic pulse.

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Think of the accent as a quick snap of the wrist, not a full arm movement. The unaccented notes should still sound clean and even.

exercises.title: Off-Beat (Upbeat) Accents
exercises.description: Now reverse it - accent the upbeats ('ands' of each beat). This is essential for reggae, ska, and funk styles. The downbeats should be quiet with strong accents on the 'and' of each beat.

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: This feels unnatural at first because we naturally accent downbeats. Start very slowly. Tap your foot on the downbeat while accenting the upbeats.

exercises.title: Basic Ghost Note Pattern
exercises.description: Ghost notes are muted, percussive notes that add rhythm and groove. Lightly rest your fretting fingers on the strings (not pressing down) and pick. Alternate between full notes on beats 1 and 3, and ghost notes on beats 2 and 4.

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Ghost notes should be barely audible - more felt than heard. They provide rhythmic momentum and make your playing groove. Think of them as the heartbeat between notes.

exercises.title: Funk Strumming with Ghosts
exercises.description: Combine full E9 chord stabs with ghost note strums. Play accented chord hits on beats 1 and the 'and' of 2, with ghost note strums filling the rest. This is the foundation of funk rhythm guitar.

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Keep your strumming hand moving in constant 16th notes (down-up-down-up). Ghost notes happen by simply relaxing fretting hand pressure. The strumming hand never stops.

items.title: Developing Dynamic Range
items: Practice unplugged to develop acoustic dynamic awareness
The best players use dynamics to tell a story within a song
Start every session with volume control exercises for 2-3 minutes
Listen to funk masters like Nile Rodgers and James Brown's guitarists for ghost note inspiration

items.title: Common Dynamic Mistakes
items: Playing at a single volume level (the most common mistake)
Tensing up when trying to play quietly - relaxation is key
Making ghost notes too loud (they should be barely audible)
Rushing accents - keep the tempo steady regardless of dynamics
